title: File upload (multipart, size limits), streaming download, SSE, WebSockets
summary: Request and response bodies are streams: read uploads part by part under a size cap, write downloads and Server-Sent Events as they are produced, and flush. WebSockets leave HTTP after a 101 handshake; the standard library stops there.

examples.title: Streaming a multipart upload under a size limit

annotations.note: The cap goes on the whole body before anything reads it. Every part, header and boundary counts, so one limit covers files and fields.

MultipartReader hands out parts in order as they arrive. Its alternative, ParseMultipartForm (also called by r.FormValue and r.FormFile, with 32 MB of memory), reads the whole body first: memory up to the limit, temp files for the rest.
On HTTP/1.x a handler should finish reading the body before it writes the response. Collecting the report and writing it at the end also keeps a 413 possible until the last byte.
io.Copy moves the part in 32 KiB chunks straight into the hash. Swap the hash for an os.File from os.CreateTemp or an object-storage writer and memory use stays the same for a 5 GB file.

FileName() is the client's claim, passed through filepath.Base, which depends on the OS. "../../etc/passwd" arrives as "passwd". Never use it as a path: store under a name you generate, and keep the original (here "rapor-İş.csv", UTF-8) only as metadata.
The client streams too: multipart.Writer writes into a pipe from a goroutine while http.Post reads the other end. Closing the pipe with mw.Close()'s error ends the body, or fails it.
200,000 bytes against a 64 KiB cap: the server stops reading, answers 413 and closes the connection. Go's client returns that response even though it never finished sending the body.

examples.title: Server-Sent Events: flush per event, stop when the client leaves

annotations.note: text/event-stream is what makes a browser's EventSource accept the response. no-cache keeps proxies and the browser from storing a live stream.
The wire format: "field: value" lines, a blank line ends the event. id lets EventSource send Last-Event-ID when it reconnects, so the server can resume; event picks the listener; data is the payload.
Without Flush the event sits in a 4 KiB buffer until it fills. ResponseController.Flush reports when flushing is impossible, for example behind a middleware wrapper without Unwrap.
A stream runs until someone ends it. The request context is canceled when the client disconnects, so the select is the only way out. Without it this goroutine would loop forever.
No Content-Length (-1), so HTTP/1.1 uses chunked encoding: each flush sends a chunk. Any download written with io.Copy(w, src) without a length is streamed the same way.
Canceling the request context closes the connection. The server notices only because it was waiting on r.Context().Done(); a handler that never looks would find out at its next failed write.

examples.title: The WebSocket upgrade handshake with net/http, and one raw frame

annotations.note: The only cryptography in the handshake, and it isn't security: it proves the server understood the WebSocket request, so a misconfigured plain HTTP server can't accidentally accept one.
426 Upgrade Required with an Upgrade header tells a plain HTTP client which protocol this endpoint wants.

Browsers send Origin on WebSocket requests but enforce nothing, so checking it is the server's job. Skipping the check enables cross-site WebSocket hijacking: another site's page opens a socket with your user's cookies.
Hijack takes the TCP connection away from net/http: no more headers, timeouts or Shutdown tracking. It works only on HTTP/1.x; HTTP/2 connections don't support it.
A minimal frame: FIN plus opcode 1 (text), then a length byte. The length counts bytes: "Merhaba dünya" is 14 bytes but 13 characters, and text frames must be valid UTF-8.
The sample key from RFC 6455. Real clients send 16 random bytes in base64; the expected accept value s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo= is printed in the RFC and on MDN, so you can check the computation.
Since Go 1.12 the client hands back a 101 response whose Body is also an io.Writer: the raw connection, readable and writable.

use_cases: Uploads of CSV imports, images and documents, written to disk or object storage without holding them in memory
Exports and backups streamed with io.Copy or http.ServeContent (which adds Range and conditional requests)
SSE for one-way live updates: job progress, notifications, log tails, LLM token streams
WebSockets for two-way, low-latency traffic: chat, collaborative editing, games
strengths: io.Reader and io.Writer make streaming the default shape: MultipartReader, io.Copy and Flush compose without callbacks, unlike Node's stream events or Java's servlet async API
Size limits are one wrapper (MaxBytesReader) with a typed error
SSE needs nothing beyond net/http: a header, a format and Flush; the browser's EventSource adds reconnection and Last-Event-ID for free
weaknesses: No WebSocket implementation in the standard library: Hijack gives you a raw connection, and framing, masking, ping/pong and the close handshake are a library's job
Hijacked connections are invisible to Server.Shutdown and to server timeouts; you manage their lifecycle yourself
Streams fight with server-wide WriteTimeout, TimeoutHandler and buffering middleware such as compression, which need per-route exceptions
SSE is one-way, text-only, and over HTTP/1.1 limited to six connections per browser and domain

pitfalls.title: r.FormValue on an upload endpoint
pitfalls.detail: It calls ParseMultipartForm(32 MB) for you: up to 32 MB in memory and the rest in temp files, before your code sees a byte. Use MultipartReader for large or untrusted uploads.

pitfalls.title: Trusting the file name and Content-Type of a part
pitfalls.detail: Both come from the client. Generate the storage name, keep the original for display, and sniff the type with http.DetectContentType on the first 512 bytes if it matters.
pitfalls.good: f, err := os.CreateTemp(dir, "upload-*") // original name goes to metadata

pitfalls.title: Writing an SSE stream without Flush
pitfalls.detail: The events wait in the server's buffer and arrive in bursts or at the end. Flush after every event, and check that no middleware hides Flush.

pitfalls.title: A non-ASCII download name in Content-Disposition
pitfalls.detail: filename="rapor-İş.csv" in a raw header is not portable. mime.FormatMediaType("attachment", map[string]string{"filename": name}) produces filename*=utf-8''rapor-%C4%B0%C5%9F.csv, the RFC 2231 encoding browsers understand.

pitfalls.title: Accepting WebSocket upgrades from any origin
pitfalls.detail: CORS doesn't apply to WebSockets. Compare Origin against an allow-list before upgrading, or any site can open a socket with your users' cookies.

quiz.q: An upload handler calls r.FormFile("file") on a 2 GB upload. What happens before the call returns?
options: The whole body is parsed: up to 32 MB in memory, the rest in temp files
It fails: the body is too large
quiz.why: FormFile calls ParseMultipartForm with 32 MB of memory if the form isn't parsed yet, which consumes the entire body.

quiz.q: An SSE handler writes events but never calls Flush. What does the browser see?
options: Events in bursts when the buffer fills, or at the end
quiz.why: Small writes sit in the server's response buffer until it fills or the handler returns; Flush pushes them out.

quiz.q: Which statement about WebSockets in Go's standard library is true?
options: net/http can perform the upgrade through Hijack, but framing, masking and control frames need code of your own or a library
quiz.why: The standard library has no WebSocket package; after the 101 the connection is yours. Shutdown doesn't track hijacked connections.

quiz.q: Why must a WebSocket server check the Origin header itself?
options: Browsers don't send Origin on WebSocket requests
Browsers don't apply CORS to WebSocket connections
quiz.why: Browsers send Origin but don't block the connection; without a server-side check, any site can connect with the user's cookies (cross-site WebSocket hijacking).

further_reading.title: package golang.org/x/net/websocket (and the alternatives its docs recommend)

body:
## Concept

A request body is an `io.Reader` and a response is an `io.Writer`. As long as you keep
them that way, memory use doesn't depend on the size of what passes through. Buffering
creeps in through convenient calls: `io.ReadAll(r.Body)`, `r.FormFile`, a JSON encoder
fed one giant slice.

**Uploads.** Cap the body with `http.MaxBytesReader`, then walk the parts with
`r.MultipartReader()` and `NextPart()`, copying each file part into its destination with
`io.Copy`. Exceeding the cap surfaces as `*http.MaxBytesError`: answer 413.

**Downloads.** `io.Copy(w, src)` streams. Without a known length, HTTP/1.1 switches to
chunked encoding. For files and seekable data, `http.ServeContent` adds `Content-Length`,
range requests (resumable downloads) and conditional GETs.

**Server-Sent Events.** A response that never ends: `Content-Type: text/event-stream`,
events made of `id:`, `event:` and `data:` lines, each event ended by a blank line and
followed by a `Flush`. The browser's `EventSource` parses them, and reconnects on its own
with a `Last-Event-ID` header. A line starting with `:` is a comment, useful as a
keep-alive through proxies.

**WebSockets.** A GET with `Upgrade: websocket` and a random `Sec-WebSocket-Key`; the server
answers `101 Switching Protocols` with `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`, and from then on both sides
exchange binary frames on the same TCP connection. `net/http` gets you to the 101 through
`Hijack`. Everything after it is yours or a library's.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Node**: `req` and `res` are streams there too, and `busboy` or `multer` stream
  multipart. `res.write` + `res.flushHeaders` is the SSE counterpart. `ws` and Socket.IO
  are separate packages, as in Go.
- **Java**: Servlet 3.0's `request.getParts()` buffers to disk like `ParseMultipartForm`;
  Spring's `SseEmitter` wraps the SSE format. Java EE/Jakarta has a standard WebSocket API
  (JSR 356), which Go's standard library has no equivalent of.
- **Python**: Starlette's `StreamingResponse` and `request.stream()` play the same roles;
  WebSockets need an ASGI server, never WSGI.
- **C/C++**: think `sendfile` and a write loop; `io.Copy` uses such fast paths when both
  sides allow it.

## How it works

What a WebSocket library adds after the handshake, all of it from RFC 6455:

- **Masking**: client-to-server frames are XOR-masked with a fresh 4-byte key, and a server
  must close the connection on an unmasked client frame. Server frames are unmasked.
- **Lengths**: 0-125 fit in the second byte; 126 means a 16-bit length follows, 127 a
  64-bit one.
- **Fragmentation**: a message may span frames (opcode 0, continuation), the last with FIN.
- **Control frames**: ping (0x9), pong (0xA) and close (0x8) with a status code and the
  close handshake; pings keep idle connections alive through NATs and proxies.
- **Checks and limits**: UTF-8 validation of text messages, maximum message sizes, one
  writer at a time per connection, optional `permessage-deflate` compression, Origin
  checks and subprotocol negotiation.

`golang.org/x/net/websocket` exists outside the standard library, and its own documentation
points to more actively maintained packages, github.com/gorilla/websocket and
github.com/coder/websocket.

## Design notes

Choose the simplest transport that fits. Polling suits data that changes every few
minutes. SSE suits server-to-client updates: it is plain HTTP, so cookies, CORS,
compression and HTTP/2 multiplexing work unchanged, and the browser reconnects for you.
Choose WebSockets when the client sends a steady stream too, and accept the cost: a
library, Origin checks, your own heartbeat, and connections that `Shutdown` doesn't see.

Long-lived responses need the server configured for them: a write deadline extended for
that route (or none), no `TimeoutHandler`, no buffering middleware, and a context that
`RegisterOnShutdown` cancels, as in the previous lesson. For uploads, decide the limit per
endpoint, stream into the destination, and record the client's file name only as metadata.
